title: Telling the children
hookLine: telling the Sahibzade story to children, gently
tomorrow: why would a Guru give his life for a faith not his own?

lines: TWO BOYS IN FRONT OF A WALL.
TELL HER THE WAY I TOLD YOU.
cards: A gentle word for parents first: today's story is about children who died, and the whole lesson is about telling it softly.
At the field day, Simran was trying out her gurpurab guide for the youth group on her little cousin Rubi.

Rubi wandered into the hallway and stopped at a framed picture: two small boys in tall turbans, standing calm in front of a brick wall. She came back with the question kids ask at exactly the wrong moment. Who are they?
What happened to them? Simran froze. From the kitchen, Bebe called out: tell her the way I told you.

teach.b: They're the Sahibzade, the younger sons of Guru Gobind Singh: Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh.

Tradition says they and their grandmother, Mata Gujri, were taken to Sirhind, told to give up their faith, and refused, and that they died there. Here's one gentle way to tell it to a child, in three parts.
Who they were: brothers, loved, with a grandmother who stayed right beside them.

teach.h: WHAT THEY CHOSE: TO STAY THEMSELVES.
teach.b: What they chose: they kept who they were, even when it was very hard.
And who stood up for them: the Nawab of Malerkotla, a Muslim noble, who said in court that children must not be punished.
Notice what's left out: the details of the wall.
A child doesn't need them, and the story doesn't depend on them. What a child keeps is love, courage, and one person from another faith who spoke up.

how: Sikh families remember the Sahibzade each winter, around the Shaheedi Jor Mela at Fatehgarh Sahib; with young children, some parents and gurdwara classes tell the story through the boys' courage and their grandmother's care.

o: a children's class where kids memorize the hymns
sharing the Sahibzade story with kids, honestly and gently
keeping hard stories from kids until they're grown

games.q: the week, lived — tap the pairs.

s: children should hear every detail of the Sahibzade story
a child keeps love, courage and the Nawab who spoke up; the wall can wait.
the Nawab of Malerkotla spoke up for the boys
a Muslim noble said in court that children must not be punished.
a chhabeel's cold drink is meant for Sikhs only
cold water, freely: anyone in the heat gets a cup.

games.q: your friend's kid asks why the boys in the picture look so calm. which answer fits a child?
o: they were loved and brave, and they kept who they were, even when it was hard.
they were calm because they were too young to understand what was happening.
it's just a painting; artists make every face look calm.
games.why: people sometimes say the boys were too young to understand. Sikhs remember it the other way: small, and steady. a child can hold that.

practice: Say the story out loud, quietly, in three sentences, as if a child were sitting beside you: who they were, what they chose, who spoke up for them. Then say it once more, slower and softer, and let the last sentence be the Nawab's.

wordCard.voice: Telling the children. Sharing the Sahibzade's story with young ones honestly and gently: their love, their courage, and the Nawab who spoke up.

orig.note: Punjabi: the honored sons, used for Guru Gobind Singh's sons.

carryVoice: Keep this one: tell it gently, the truth without the wall. A week closes on a hallway floor.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 5, life of Guru Gobind Singh (Sirhind; the Nawab of Malerkotla's protest)
